transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 mins | Attendees: Sofia Martin (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Head of ML, Nebula), Liam Chen (Infra Lead), Marisol Vega (CTO)

[00:00] Sofia Martin: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call?
[00:05] Priya Rao: Hi, Priya here.
[00:07] Liam Chen: Liam.
[00:08] Marisol Vega: Marisol on for the CTO side.
[00:10] Ethan Park: Ethan from Redwood SE.
[00:12] Sofia Martin: Cool, thanks. We scheduled 45, looks like we have a bit more, 52 minutes. The plan is to go through how you'd integrate -- SDKs, any LangChain or LlamaIndex work, gateway/proxy patterns for routing between hosted/dedicated/private, and observability/rate limit questions. Sound good?

[00:30] Priya Rao: Yep, that's the ask. We're evaluating Redwood because of the latency/cost story. Primary use case is real-time enrichment of customer chats and a nightly batch embedding job.

[00:42] Marisol Vega: Security is huge, we may need VPC and KMS integration if we go to production. Also interested in telemetry hooks for cost allocation per team.

[01:05] Sofia Martin: Got it. Ethan, want to run us through SDKs and the LangChain pieces?

[01:12] Ethan Park: Sure. Official SDKs are in Python and Node; they wrap the REST endpoints and support streaming, function calls, embeddings. For LangChain and LlamaIndex we have connector examples — some customers use our direct client inside LangChain chains, others use a small gateway/proxy to do routing. The examples repo has a LangChain integration and a LlamaIndex notebook. I'll share the links.

[01:35] Liam Chen: So if we have an internal pipeline using LangChain, do we need to change our chain code to talk to Redwood or can it go through our existing inference gateway?

[01:45] Ethan Park: Both are possible. Two patterns we've seen: 1) Call Redwood directly from the app/chain (SDK) — simplest. 2) Route via your gateway/proxy to centralize auth, quota tracking, and internal caching. Our clients accept standard REST calls, so your gateway can translate and forward. Important note: for Dedicated/Private, you can run Redwood's private agent inside your VPC so traffic never leaves your network.

[02:10] Priya Rao: About caching — we use prefix reuse a lot. Does Redwood support KV cache or prefix cache natively? We heard something like KV cash in a blog (laughs).

[02:20] Ethan Park: Yep, KV cache — sorry KV cash — so our serving runtime supports prefix/KV caching; the Dedicated runtime also exposes hooks for your gateway to warm or invalidate cache. For example, if you run a sidecar gateway you can push cached KV pairs. There might be some slight term mismatch in docs; we'll send a clearer note.

[02:40] Marisol Vega: For observability, we need traces across our app -> gateway -> Redwood, and token-level cost attribution. How granular is your tracing?

[02:50] Ethan Park: We export traces via OpenTelemetry and provide per-request metadata that includes token usage, model variant, latency breakdown (tokenization, decode, kernel time). You can ingest those into your tracing backend. For cost, the Console has token-level cost breakdowns by API key/route. If you proxy through a single key, you can pass internal route tags so costs attribute to teams.

[03:18] Priya Rao: SSO & audit logs — we need SAML SSO and long-term audit retention for compliance.

[03:25] Sofia Martin: For Hosted we have SAML for the Console and audit logs with configurable retention as an add-on. For Dedicated and Private you can control retention and integrate with your SIEM; Private gives you the most control (KMS/HSM integration, VPC). We'll share the SOC2/ISO docs.

[03:45] Liam Chen: Rate limits: our traffic spikes a lot; we need predictable throttling per team with burst capacity. How does Redwood handle quotas?

[03:55] Ethan Park: On Hosted, rate limits are per API key with adjustable quotas and burst windows; Dedicated gives you capacity reservation and per-route quotas. You can also set global and per-API-key rate limits and fallback policies — e.g., route to a smaller model variant when capacity constrained. For Dedicated, we can configure autoscaling with burst capacity, but you define SLOs.

[04:25] Marisol Vega: That fallback behavior interests us. If latency goes high, can we auto-fallback to a faster quantized model?

[04:33] Ethan Park: Yep, smart routing supports model variants. You define compatible variants in the rollout policy; the runtime can transparently fall back to a configured variant if the primary is overloaded. There is some quality tradeoff, so your evals should include rollback thresholds.

[04:55] Priya Rao: About LlamaIndex — our embeddings pipeline uses a custom embedding model today. Will you let us host custom models on Dedicated/Private?

[05:05] Ethan Park: Dedicated supports customer-provided model artifacts in many cases; Private definitely can. There are constraints depending on licensing and format. We help with model onboarding and kernel selection. For Hosted we offer curated open models but not arbitrary customer hosts.

[05:30] Liam Chen: We run everything in our GCP project. For Private, do you provide an appliance or an operator? What's the install pattern?

[05:38] Sofia Martin: Private ships as a control plane with an on-prem agent/operator; you can run it in your VPC or on prem. There's an install guide: Helm charts for k8s or a packaged image for air-gapped installs. The control plane still can be customer-managed. We'll send the architecture doc.

[05:58] Marisol Vega: Latency targets — we need P95 under 250ms for the 512-token path. Any benchmarks?

[06:06] Ethan Park: We have verified performance profiles per model and per GPU type; those are in the model catalog. P95 will depend on sequence length and batching — Dedicated tuned kernels usually hit those numbers for smaller sequences. We'll add a note: benchmark we run with similar traffic and show P95 numbers. We'll also run a Nebula-specific benchmark if you provide a sample workload.

[06:30] Priya Rao: Pricing — if we start with Hosted then move to Dedicated, how does commit/credits work?

[06:38] Sofia Martin: Hosted is pay-as-you-go. For Dedicated there's a reserved capacity contract with commit tiers; you can transition credits. We'll send the pricing worksheet that shows per-token cost at various commit levels and expected unit economics with batching/quantization suggestions.

[06:58] Liam Chen: About SDKs — do the SDKs support automatic retries, idempotency keys, and streaming reassembly? Our gateway needs those features.

[07:08] Ethan Park: Yes: SDKs support retry/backoff, idempotency keys for non-streaming calls, and streaming is chunked with event IDs for reassembly. If you sit behind a proxy that slices streams, you might handle reassembly at the gateway.

[07:30] Priya Rao: Can we tag requests for cost allocation from our microservices?

[07:34] Sofia Martin: Absolutely. You can add metadata headers that surface in Console reporting. For per-team cost allocation we recommend issuing team-scoped API keys or adding the route tag header.

[07:50] Marisol Vega: A couple of red flags: encryption in transit and at rest, and KMS integration for Dedicated.

[07:58] Ethan Park: TLS is standard in transit. For at-rest we use customer-managed keys (CMK) for Private/Dedicated with KMS/HSM integrations. We'll send the KMS integration docs.

[08:18] Priya Rao: Ok can we walk through a sample flow the way we'd implement it? Say we have a LangChain agent that calls Redwood for LLM and our embedding pipeline that writes embeddings to Pinecone — but we want Redwood to produce embeddings.

[08:30] Ethan Park: Sure. Option A: In the chain, swap out the embedder to call Redwood embeddings endpoint directly — minimal changes. Option B: Keep your internal embedder service and have it proxy calls, adding per-team tags and doing caching. If you want isolation, run Dedicated in a VPC and have the embedder service call the private endpoint. We also have sample code showing LangChain integration in the examples repo — note, some of the connector names are slightly different in the repo, e.g., "redwood-client" vs internal examples; we'll make that consistent.

[09:05] Priya Rao: Are there official LangChain or LlamaIndex wrappers?

[09:10] Ethan Park: We maintain a community-supported LangChain adapter and a LlamaIndex notebook; it's in the repo. For production you'd probably vendor a small adapter in your repo to lock behavior. We'll provide code snippets.

[09:32] Liam Chen: On quotas, if we want per-team throttling, is it better to manage that in our gateway or use Redwood's per-key quotas?

[09:40] Ethan Park: Either works. Using Redwood quotas simplifies enforcement on the service side and gives automatic throttling under overload. Gateway-based quotas let you implement custom queueing/backpressure and maintain internal SLAs. Many customers use a combination: gateway enforces soft limits, Redwood enforces hard limits.

[10:02] Marisol Vega: Are there any gotchas with function calling or structured outputs, particularly with streams?

[10:09] Ethan Park: Function calling works with streaming; you get incremental tokens and can parse partial JSON. Edge cases: partial JSON chunks can arrive — SDKs provide utilities for safe parsing/reassembly. We'll include the best practices doc.

[10:28] Priya Rao: Can we do a short demo of the SDK call now?

[10:32] Sofia Martin: We can demo a quick curl or Python, but Ethan has the code snippets. Ethan, wanna share screen for 2 minutes?

[10:36] Ethan Park: Quick demo: Python snippet to init client with API key, call chat.create with streaming callback. [screen share shown briefly; audio notes] Code shows streaming callback printing tokens; you can pass metadata headers for route tagging.

[12:00] Priya Rao: Nice. That looks straightforward. On the security front, can we get SOC2/ISO docs and the Private network architecture?

[12:10] Sofia Martin: Yes, will attach SOC2 report, ISO brief, and Private deployment architecture in the follow up.

[12:20] Liam Chen: For the POC, we want to run a 2-week pilot: 1) run our nightly embeddings, 2) run production-like chat load (simulated) to measure P95 and cost. What data do you need?

[12:30] Ethan Park: We'll need sample payloads, expected concurrency, sequence-length distribution, and a test S3 bucket with representative documents. If you want Private/Dedicated pilot we'll coordinate infra access and an install window.

[12:52] Priya Rao: About the install window — we prefer late May.

[12:55] Sofia Martin: Noted. We'll try to align a Dedicated/Private install in the 2nd half of May if the legal/contract runs quickly.

[13:10] Marisol Vega: Any limitations on model quantization or custom kernels with Private?

[13:16] Ethan Park: You can use quantized models; Private lets you deploy custom kernels subject to compatibility. We'll vet the format. For certain proprietary kernels we may need a separate validation pass.

[13:30] Priya Rao: Okay, last question: how do we instrument per-request metadata so our billing and observability matches our internal tenants?

[13:36] Ethan Park: Add X-Redwood-Meta headers with JSON-safe tags or set per-request metadata fields in SDK calls. Console and telemetry export include those fields for attribution. If you funnel through a proxy, ensure it forwards headers.

[13:55] Liam Chen: Great. Any other questions?

[14:00] Marisol Vega: No, looks good.

[14:05] Sofia Martin: Recap: We'll send pricing worksheet, SOC2/ISO & KMS docs, LangChain/LlamaIndex quickstarts, and schedule a POC planning call. Nebula will provide sample workload and confirm late-May install window. Action items recorded in the chat.

[14:25] Priya Rao: Sounds good; thanks.

[14:28] Sofia Martin: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.

[14:35] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings ("KV cash" for KV cache), minor speaker overlaps. The conversation included explicit asks: LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy vs direct SDK tradeoffs, Dedicated capacity with burst autoscaling, Private/VPC install options, per-team quotas, OpenTelemetry traces, token-level cost attribution, SOC2/KMS docs.

End of transcript.
